claims.text: The alloy begins in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
Aging at high temperature causes the metastable alloy to evolve toward a more stable microstructure by precipitating intermetallic compounds.
The intermetallic compounds precipitate from a supersaturated solid solution.
Intermetallic precipitation affects the alloy's corrosion resistance.
Intermetallic precipitation affects the alloy's high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Whether corrosion resistance is retained or lost depends on the type and distribution of the precipitated intermetallic compounds.
Whether high-temperature oxidation resistance is retained or lost depends on the type and distribution of the precipitated intermetallic compounds.
Temperature and aging time bound the regime in which intermetallic precipitation occurs.
The exact transformation pathway and kinetics are uncertain because of the complexity of the alloy system.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing aged samples with unaged samples using TEM, XRD, corrosion testing, and high-temperature oxidation testing.
The hypothesis is falsified if aging produces no significant difference in either microstructure or corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to unaged samples.
